Later anthropological work on Tiwi society, including Jane Goodale's, provides broader context on ceremony and social organisation.

Contemporary Tiwi art centres and artists are the appropriate living source. Tiwi Design and Munupi and Jilamara art centres represent artists working in these traditions today.
sections.disputed:
The publicly available description rests on a narrow and dated ethnographic base, and should not be treated as comprehensive or authoritative.

Cultural protocols apply to much Tiwi knowledge, including restrictions on who may know or repeat certain material. Absence from published sources is not evidence of absence, and is frequently evidence of appropriate restriction.

The one-eye resemblance to Polyphemus, the ojancanu and other figures is real as a description but should not be read as connection. There is no plausible transmission, and the recurrence more likely reflects something about how humans imagine an inhuman face.

This entry is written from outside the culture on the basis of limited sources, and says so.

fate: Not recorded in the sources available to us.
communityNote: Whether this material should appear in a general catalogue at all is a fair question. We have kept a short entry rather than deleting it silently, because the gap and the reason for it are worth showing, but we would remove or correct it on request from the relevant community. Requests can be sent to hello@giantscodex.com.

name: Murkupang
shortDescription: Giant figure in northern Australian story cycles of pursuit and country.
fullDescription: Murkupang is a cannibal giant recorded in Australian Aboriginal tradition, hunting people and taking children. The external record is thin, and this entry is correspondingly short.
mysteryNote: Follow the story only as far as Country allows. The map is not entitled to everything.
sources: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition (community not reliably identified in available sources)
20th-c. compilations of Australian Aboriginal legend: unreliable, see disputed
AIATSIS protocols for Indigenous knowledge

sections.story:
Accounts describe Murkupang as an enormous being who preys on people, and particularly on children: the standard shape of a cannibal-giant tradition, of which Australia has many, held by many different peoples with distinct languages and laws.

We are going to be brief, and the reason is the reason we gave for Nawao.

"Australian Aboriginal" is not one culture. It covers hundreds of distinct nations and language groups with separate traditions, and the material recorded under a single name in colonial-era or mid-century compilations has frequently been detached from the specific people it belongs to. That has happened here: the sources available to us do not reliably identify the community whose tradition this is, which means we cannot attribute it properly, and improper attribution is not a small error.

A great deal of Australian material was also recorded by people who assumed the cultures were dying, who did not seek permission, and who published knowledge that was restricted. Some of what circulates in general reference works should not be in general reference works.

What can be said: cannibal-giant figures are widespread in Aboriginal traditions across the continent; they commonly function partly as warnings to children about wandering and about specific dangerous country; and they belong to living cultures whose members are the appropriate authority.

What we will not do is compose a detailed portrait to fill the space. If you hold this tradition and we have it wrong, or should not be carrying it at all, please write to us.
sections.origins:
Australian Aboriginal oral tradition; the specific community is not reliably identified in the sources available to us, which is itself the problem this entry describes.

The name appears in twentieth-century compilations of Australian Aboriginal legend, a genre that frequently aggregated material across unrelated peoples without adequate attribution.

Community-controlled sources, language centres and Indigenous knowledge bodies are the appropriate authority for any specific tradition.

AIATSIS, the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies, maintains protocols and collections relevant to this material.
sections.disputed:
Attribution is the central problem. Without knowing which people's tradition this is, nothing further can responsibly be said about context, meaning or restriction.

Popular compilations of "Aboriginal legends" published through the twentieth century are unreliable as sources. They routinely merged distinct traditions, removed cultural context, and were often published without consent.

Whether this material should appear in a general catalogue at all is a fair question. We have kept a short entry rather than deleting it silently, because the gap and the reason for it are worth showing, but we would remove or correct it on request from the relevant community. Requests can be sent to hello@giantscodex.com.

fate: Not recorded in the sources available to us.

name: Thardid Jimbo
shortDescription: Cannibal giant of southeastern Aboriginal tales: a terror of the camp edge.
fullDescription: Thardid Jimbo is recorded as a giant of Australian Aboriginal tradition, over two metres tall, who hunted people and was killed after taking a woman as a wife. The record has the same attribution problems as its neighbours.
mysteryNote: Stay near the fire. The dark has a name in more than one language, and more than one warning.
sources: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition (community not reliably identified)
20th-c. legend compilations: unreliable, see disputed
AIATSIS protocols for Indigenous knowledge
imageAlt: A gaunt towering figure stalking through red desert scrub at dusk, dust rising around its legs and dead trees on the horizon

sections.story:
The narrative recorded under this name describes a large man-eating being who takes a woman, in some tellings a woman already married, and is eventually killed, in several versions after his intended prey or her kin outwit him.

As with Murkupang, the material reaches general reference through twentieth-century compilations that did not adequately identify the community it came from, and we are not able to attribute it with confidence.

There is a general point worth making here rather than repeating it entry by entry.

Australian Aboriginal cultures are the oldest continuous cultures on earth, with traditions that in documented cases, Budj Bim in this same codex, preserve accurate memory of events tens of thousands of years old. They are not a source of generic monster stories. Treating them as raw material for a curiosity catalogue, which is exactly what much of the twentieth-century publishing did, is both inaccurate and disrespectful.

The cannibal-giant figures are real traditions with real functions: marking dangerous country, instructing children, encoding law. Detached from the people, the place and the language, almost all of that is lost, and what remains is a monster with a name.

We are keeping short entries for these rather than removing them, so that the shape of the problem stays visible instead of being tidied away. Fuller and better-sourced treatment would require working with the relevant communities, which is a real undertaking and not one we can shortcut.

The name appears in mid-twentieth-century compilations of Australian Aboriginal legend, with the attribution and consent problems described above.

Community-controlled sources and language centres are the appropriate authority.

AIATSIS holds relevant collections and maintains protocols governing use of Indigenous knowledge.
sections.disputed:
The same attribution failure applies as to Murkupang, and it is not a minor caveat: it means we cannot say whose story this is.

The published versions vary in detail, and the variation cannot be assessed without knowing the source traditions.

Some Australian Aboriginal knowledge is restricted by law and custom, including by gender and initiation status. General publication of such material has caused real harm, and reference works have participated in it.

This entry exists to hold the place and state the problem. It should not be read as an account of the tradition.

name: Chinny-kinik
shortDescription: Giant being in Aboriginal narrative: sparse in print, strong in place.
fullDescription: Chinny-Kinik is recorded as a giant of Australian Aboriginal tradition. As with the other entries in this group, the external record is thin and the attribution unreliable.
mysteryNote: Some names are doors. This catalogue only knocks, and does not pretend to hold the key.
sources: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition (community not reliably identified)
20th-c. legend compilations: unreliable, see disputed
AIATSIS protocols for Indigenous knowledge

sections.story:
The published material describes a large hostile being of the same broad type as the other Australian entries here: dangerous to people, associated with particular country, defeated or escaped through wit.

We are treating this the same way, and for the same reasons set out under Murkupang and Thardid Jimbo: we cannot reliably identify the community whose tradition this is, and without that, a detailed account would be fabrication dressed as scholarship.

There is one further thing worth recording, which applies to this whole group.

The codex currently carries these entries because the original catalogue did, and the original catalogue took them from the general literature. That literature is not good. A responsible version of this section would be built by approaching the relevant communities, asking whether they wish the material published, and following their answer: including if the answer is no.

Until that work is done, these are placeholders with an honest label rather than entries with content.

A reader who wants to understand Aboriginal traditions of large beings would be far better served by community-published material, by AIATSIS resources, and by Aboriginal authors writing about their own countries, than by anything this page can offer.

The honest position is that this entry records that a tradition exists under approximately this name, and nothing more. We would rather publish that than a confident paragraph we invented.

name: Maero
shortDescription: Wild folk of the forest in Māori tradition: long fingers, fierce, untamed.
fullDescription: Maero are wild forest beings of Maori tradition: hairy, with long bony fingers ending in claws, living apart in the bush and hostile to people who enter it.
mysteryNote: The bush does not need to be taller than you to be larger than you. The maero already knew.
sources: Maori oral tradition (varies by iwi)
John White, The Ancient History of the Maori (1887-90): period-bound
Elsdon Best, ethnographic writings on Maori forest lore, early 20th c.
Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

sections.story:
Maori tradition includes several kinds of being associated with the forest interior and with places away from settlement, and the maero is among the more consistently hostile.

Descriptions give them a covering of hair, great strength, and long fingers with hard nails or claws used as weapons. They live in the deep bush and in rough country, alone or in small numbers rather than as a people. Encounters go badly for the person who has the encounter.

They are frequently mentioned alongside other beings of the interior (the ponaturi, the tipua, and various named entities associated with particular places), and the boundaries between these categories are not sharp and vary between iwi.

The function is recognisable across many traditions with forested or mountainous interiors: the bush beyond the cleared land is not empty, it is occupied, and it is not friendly. That is both a story and, in country like the New Zealand interior, sound advice.

As with the other Maori material in this codex, most of what reaches English-language reference works passes through nineteenth-century colonial collection, with the distortions that involves: including the standard settler habit of filing distinct beings under "giant" or "wild man" because those were the available categories.

Accounts differ between iwi and between tellings, and there is no single canonical maero. Maori sources are the authority here, not this one.
sections.origins:
Maori oral tradition, with variation between iwi.

Nineteenth-century collection, including material gathered by John White in The Ancient History of the Maori and by other settler-era compilers, is the main published English-language route and carries the problems of that period.

Elsdon Best's early twentieth-century ethnographic writing covers forest beings extensively and is widely cited, though his framing reflects his time.

Contemporary Maori scholarship, iwi sources and Te Ara, the online Encyclopedia of New Zealand, are better starting points for current understanding.
sections.disputed:
Categories overlap. Maero, tipua, ponaturi and related beings are distinguished differently in different traditions, and English-language sources have frequently merged them.

The colonial collections that carry most of this material into English were shaped by their compilers' assumptions and sometimes by their politics, and cannot be read as neutral transcription.

Occasional attempts to link maero traditions to a real relict population, or to cryptozoology, have no support and repeat a nineteenth-century error.

Variation between iwi is substantial and any single description, including this one, flattens it.

fate: No fixed fate; encounters end however the individual story requires.

name: Kahui-Tipua
shortDescription: Bands of supernatural giants in Māori tradition: tipua of collective power.
fullDescription: The Kāhui Tipua are a band of supernatural giants in southern Māori tradition, credited with shaping parts of the South Island landscape: including, in some accounts, the excavation of the great lakes.
mysteryNote: Before the maps, the bands walked. Some say they never stopped: only stepped sideways out of ordinary sight.
sources: Southern Māori oral tradition (Ngāi Tahu; earlier Waitaha and Kati Mamoe)
Herries Beattie, "Nature-lore of the Southern Maori", Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute 52 (1920)
Ngāi Tahu published sources and Claims Settlement documentation
Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand
James W. Stack, "Sketch of the Traditional History of the South Island Maoris", Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute 10 (1877)

sections.story:
Tipua is a term for beings or objects of supernatural power, and the Kāhui Tipua are an assemblage of such beings in the traditions of the southern South Island, particularly among Ngāi Tahu and the earlier peoples whose traditions Ngāi Tahu carry.

James W. Stack, writing in 1877, described them as giants who could stride from mountain range to mountain range, swallow rivers, and transform themselves into anything animate or inanimate that they chose. Accounts associate them with the making of major features of Te Waipounamu, the South Island.

The best-known material of this kind concerns the southern lakes. Traditions attach the formation of Lake Wakatipu, and in some versions other lakes, to the actions of great beings: the most widely repeated being the story of Matau, a giant whose burning body left the hollow the lake fills, with the rise and fall of the water explained as his heart still beating. Different accounts and different iwi tell this differently, and Matau is not always grouped with the Kāhui Tipua.

What holds these together is a way of reading the country. The South Island landscape is dramatic (deep glacial lakes, fault-driven mountains), and southern Māori tradition accounts for it through the actions of beings of the appropriate scale. The features are the evidence and the record at once.

The formal geological account, of glaciation and tectonics, is not in competition with this. They are answering different questions, and only one of them was available for most of human history.

The best-attested individual of the group is Kōpūwai, a dog-headed tipua of Central Otago and the Maniototo who kept a pack of two-headed dogs. He is called the water swallower because he swallowed the whole Mata-au, the Clutha, hunting for Kaiamio, a woman he had taken from near Kaitangata.
sections.origins:
Southern Māori oral tradition, particularly Ngāi Tahu, carrying earlier Waitaha and Kati Mamoe traditions. These are distinct peoples whose histories are layered in the south, and the traditions reflect that layering rather than a single line of descent.

Nineteenth-century collection includes material recorded by settler-era compilers, with the usual caveats about selection and framing. Herries Beattie's twentieth-century work on southern Māori tradition, based on extensive interviews with elders in Otago and Southland, is frequently cited and remains a substantial body of record.

Ngāi Tahu published sources are the authoritative modern reference. The Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act of 1998 formally recognises traditional associations with named landscape features and restored a number of Māori place-names in dual form, which gives some of this material a standing in New Zealand law as well as in tradition.

Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, provides accessible summary material and is a reasonable starting point for a general reader.

The name is not only southern. In Te Tau Ihu, at the top of the South Island, the Kāhui Tipua are remembered as an ancient tribe of ogres and giants living at the Wairau who impeded Kupe's exploration. He destroyed them by swamping their villages as he made Kāpara-te-hau, the lagoons now called Lake Grassmere.

Ngāi Tahu material describes the Kāhui Tipua as the first inhabitants of the South Island and as a hapū of the Maeroero, which places them in the same family as the maero of the forest interior.
sections.disputed:
The composition of the Kāhui Tipua and which beings belong to it differ between accounts, and the term is used with varying breadth.

The relationship between the Kāhui Tipua and the Matau lake tradition is not consistent across sources; treating them as a single body of story is a simplification.

Southern Māori traditions were disrupted by nineteenth-century population loss and displacement, and much of the surviving published record was collected late and by outsiders.

Attempts to read these traditions as encoded geology, as memories of actual glacial or seismic events, are occasionally made. Unlike the Budj Bim case, there is no dating evidence supporting such a reading here, and it should be treated as speculation.

Beattie's published work names very few of the people he recorded. Most appear as "one old Maori" or "my informant", with occasional exceptions such as Tare Te Maiharoa and Reko. The material is substantial and the chain of custody is not.

fate: No single fate; some became the landscape itself.

name: Nawao
shortDescription: Wild people of early Aotearoa tradition: forest dwellers of great strength.
fullDescription: The Nawao are described in some Māori traditions as a wild, strong people of the interior forests: sometimes framed as an earlier group overcome or absorbed in ancestral history. Accounts vary, and colonial-era writing distorted them badly.
mysteryNote: Strength in the trees. Memory in the names. Both outlast the clearing, and the cartoon versions.
sources: Māori oral tradition (varies by iwi; not a single canonical account)
19th-c. settler-era compilations - preserved and distorted the material; treat with caution
Later scholarship rejecting the pre-Māori settlement thesis

sections.story:
Some Māori traditions speak of the Nawao as a people of the interior: large, strong, living apart in the forested inland country, and encountered by ancestors who came later. In the accounts that reach us they are overcome, absorbed, or simply cease to be met.

They are not a single fixed figure. Different iwi and different tellings place them differently, and the name appears alongside other terms for earlier or wild peoples of the interior. What the traditions consistently carry is a relationship, between people who arrived and something already inland, rather than a creature with a stable description.

That distinction matters here more than usual, because the interesting question about the Nawao is not what they looked like. It is what happened to the accounts.
sections.origins:
Nearly everything written about the Nawao in English passes through nineteenth-century colonial collection, and that process was not neutral.

Settler-era writers gathering Māori material in the 1800s worked with their own categories to hand, and 'giants' was one of them. A tradition about an earlier inland people, told for reasons internal to Māori history and whakapapa, could be received by a European reader as a story about monsters, and was often printed that way. Some of that writing was also put to use supporting the idea of a pre-Māori population, a claim that served colonial land arguments and has been rejected by subsequent scholarship.

So the surviving printed record is a double object. It preserves something, and it distorts it, and the two are not easy to separate at this distance.
sections.disputed:
We are being deliberately brief here, and the reason is worth stating plainly.

This codex will not reconstruct a detailed portrait of the Nawao from thin and compromised sources. Doing so would mean filling gaps with invention and presenting it with a confidence the record does not support: which is exactly the failure this site exists to avoid.

What can be said: the traditions are real, they belong to Māori historical and mythic memory, they vary between tellings, and they were reshaped in transmission by people with other purposes. What cannot responsibly be said is how many there were, what precisely they looked like, or how the encounters ended.

Readers who want to go further should look to iwi and Māori-authored sources rather than to colonial compilations or to us. If you know this material and we have it wrong, we would like to hear from you.

fate: Unknown: the record does not say how, or whether, the encounters ended.

name: Amazimu
shortDescription: Cannibal ogres of Zulu and related folklore: shape-shifting eaters of the unwary.
fullDescription: Amazimu are cannibal ogres of Zulu and wider Nguni tradition: large, dangerous, and consistently defeated by children who pay attention.
mysteryNote: The clever child lives. The greedy giant does not always, and the tale prefers it that way.
sources: Zulu and Nguni oral tradition (izinganekwane, intsomi genres)
Henry Callaway, Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus (1868)
Harold Scheub, studies of Xhosa and Zulu oral performance (1960s onward)

sections.story:
The izimu, plural amazimu, appears throughout Zulu and related Nguni storytelling as the standard man-eating antagonist.

They are large and strong, they eat people, and in many tales they can pass as human or change shape, which is what makes them genuinely dangerous: the threat is not always visible on arrival. Some accounts give them distinguishing marks that a careful person notices in time.

The stories are overwhelmingly about children outwitting them. A child is captured and escapes by trickery; siblings rescue one another; an ogre is persuaded to look away, to open its mouth, to carry something it should not. Frequently the izimu is destroyed by its own greed or literal-mindedness. In a widespread type, a swallowed person or people are recovered alive when the ogre is cut open.

This is a body of tales told largely to and for children, and the structure delivers a consistent message: you are small, the world contains things that will eat you, and attention and cleverness are what you have.

Nguni oral tradition (Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi, Ndebele) shares a great deal of this material with local variation, and the izimu appears across it. The tales were performed, not recited: intsomi and izinganekwane are living genres with a performer, an audience and improvisation, and reading them as fixed texts loses most of the form.

The best-known collections in English come from the colonial and mission period and reflect that framing. Nguni-language sources and contemporary scholarship are the better route.
sections.origins:
Zulu and wider Nguni oral tradition, in the izinganekwane and intsomi performance genres.

Henry Callaway's Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus (1868) is the principal early published collection. Callaway was a missionary; his work is valuable and shaped by its purpose.

Later collection and scholarship, notably Harold Scheub's extensive work on Xhosa and Zulu oral performance from the 1960s onward, treats the material as performance rather than text and is a substantial advance.

Contemporary southern African scholarship and Nguni-language sources are the appropriate current reference.
sections.disputed:
The early collections were made by missionaries with an interest in the material's utility for conversion, and their selection and presentation reflect that.

Terminology varies across Nguni languages and the beings differ in detail between traditions; treating izimu as a single fixed figure across all of them is a simplification.

Whether the amazimu should be classed as giants is debatable. They are large man-eating beings, but "ogre" fits the tales better than "giant", and the classification here follows the catalogue rather than the tradition.

Reading these tales as historical memory of a hostile population is occasionally attempted and has no support.

fate: Typically destroyed by its own greed or by the child it tried to eat.

name: Giant of the Forest
shortDescription: West African forest giant of tale cycles: a being of the deep bush.
fullDescription: A giant of the forest appears in Hausa storytelling as the large, dangerous inhabitant of the bush beyond the settlement. The specific figure behind this entry is not securely identified.
mysteryNote: The path narrows. That is how you know you have been seen, and that wit will matter more than height.
sources: Hausa oral tradition (tatsuniyoyi), northern Nigeria and Niger
Frank Edgar, Litafi na Tatsuniyoyi na Hausa (1911-13)
Neil Skinner, Hausa Tales and Traditions (partial translation of Edgar)

sections.story:
Hausa oral tradition, across northern Nigeria and Niger, includes a substantial body of tatsuniyoyi: folk tales, generally told in the evening, often to children, frequently featuring a trickster, an ogre or a spirit of the bush.

The bush, daji, is a meaningful category. It is what lies beyond the cultivated and settled land, and it is where the dodo and other dangerous beings live. Dodo is the term most often rendered in English as ogre or monster: large, devouring, sometimes shape-shifting, defeated in the tales by cunning, by a clever child, or by a magical helper.

Whether the entry in this codex refers to a specific named figure or is a generic label applied to that category by an English-language source is not something we can establish. The name as we have it is descriptive rather than a transliteration, which is itself a warning sign: it suggests the figure reached the catalogue through paraphrase rather than from a Hausa source.

We are therefore keeping this short and saying what we can.

Hausa is spoken by tens of millions of people and has a large and living oral and written literature, including a substantial body of published tatsuniyoyi in Hausa. Anyone interested should go to that literature rather than to a one-line English gloss, and a properly researched version of this entry would start there.

If a Hausa-speaking reader can identify what figure this entry was meant to describe, we would like to hear from you.
sections.origins:
Hausa oral tradition (tatsuniyoyi), northern Nigeria and Niger.

Collections include Frank Edgar's Litafi na Tatsuniyoyi na Hausa (1911-13), a large early compilation in Hausa, later partly translated into English by Neil Skinner as Hausa Tales and Traditions.

Substantial Hausa-language scholarship and publishing exists and is the appropriate primary route.

The specific figure behind this catalogue entry is not identified in the sources available to us.
sections.disputed:
The identification is the problem. A descriptive English name with no Hausa form attached cannot be traced reliably, and we are not going to guess which being was intended.

The dodo of Hausa tales is a broad category rather than a single character, and its members differ between tellings and regions.

Early collections, including Edgar's, were made under colonial administration; Edgar was a colonial officer, and while his compilation is large and valuable, the circumstances of collection are relevant.

This entry is a placeholder with an honest label. It should be either properly researched from Hausa sources or removed.

fate: Not recorded: the specific tradition behind this entry is unidentified.

name: Stallo
shortDescription: Sámi giant-troll of the north: strong, dull-witted, dangerous to herders.
fullDescription: Stallo is the large, slow, dangerous being of Sámi tradition who hunts people across the winter landscape and is beaten by wit rather than strength. Circular stone foundations across northern Scandinavia are still called Stallo sites.
mysteryNote: Strong arms. Slow thoughts. The snow remembers who ran faster, and who bragged too soon.
sources: Sámi oral tradition, N. Norway, Sweden, Finland and Kola
Johan Turi, Muitalus sámiid birra (1910)
J.K. Qvigstad, Lappiske eventyr og sagn (1927-29)
Eldar Heide, 'The Wild Host and the Etymology of Sámi Stállu', Arv (2019)
J.A. Friis, Lappisk Mythologi (1871); Rolf Kjellström, Fataburen (1976)
Anders Wepsäläinen on the stállotomter (2011); Olof Holm, Fornvännen 111 (2016)
Liedgren and Bergman (2009); Bergman et al. (2008); Storli (1993-94)
Johannes Schefferus, Lapponia (1673): external account of Sámi religion, cited for collection history

sections.story:
Stallo (stallu, staalo, depending on the language and region) appears across Sámi tradition from Norway through Sweden and Finland into the Kola Peninsula. He is big, strong, rich in silver, and stupid, and he wants to eat you.

He is often described with an iron-clad or armoured appearance, sometimes with a dog companion, sometimes with a wife called Ludak or a similar name. He travels the winter country and menaces isolated households.

The stories are almost always about outwitting him. A boy sends Stallo to fetch water in a sieve. A woman swaps sleeping places so that Stallo kills his own family in the dark. Someone convinces him that a bag of stones is food, or that a frozen lake is safe, or that a reindeer track leads somewhere it does not. He is defeated by children, by women, by anyone paying attention. Physical confrontation is almost never the method.

That distribution of intelligence is the interesting thing. Stallo is enormous and armed and rich, and he consistently loses to people with none of those advantages, which reads as a fairly clear statement about who the stories were told by and about whom.

Johan Turi kept the stallos and the giants apart. In Muitalus sámiid birra, printed in 1910 and the first book written in Sámi by a Sámi, he puts the difference plainly: the giants did not hate mankind as the stallos did. The Stállu is not the Sámi giant. He is the hostile stranger, and the Sámi had giants already.

Across northern Sweden and Norway there are circular or oval stone-walled depressions, often in groups, known in Sámi as stállotomter: Stallo sites. Their function has been debated for over a century.

The stories were also practical. Stallo was used to keep children from wandering, and to explain why one should not travel alone in winter.
sections.origins:
Sámi oral tradition, recorded from the seventeenth century onward: initially by missionaries and clergy, whose accounts are shaped by their purpose, and later by ethnographers.

Johannes Schefferus's Lapponia (1673) is an early external description of Sámi belief. Later collection by Jacob Fellman, J.K. Qvigstad and others produced substantial corpora in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; Qvigstad's Lappiske eventyr og sagn is a major compilation.

The stállotomter have been archaeologically investigated since the early twentieth century, with excavation and dating work continuing.

Contemporary Sámi writers and artists have engaged with the figure directly.

Johan Turi's Muitalus sámiid birra, 1910, is the first book written in Sámi by a Sámi. It is the point where the tradition is described from inside rather than collected from outside, and it is the source for the distinction between the stallos and the giants.
sections.disputed:
What the stállotomter are has a live argument attached, and both sides are named. Anders Wepsäläinen argued in 2011 that they are Norse, and kin to Icelandic turf houses. Olof Holm answered in Fornvännen in 2016 that they are Sámi, because the hearths run across the width of the floor and sit in the centre, which is not how the Norse houses are built. Liedgren and Bergman in 2009, Bergman and others in 2008, and Storli in 1993 to 1994 stand on the Sámi side. Their association with the Stállu of story is a folk attribution, not an archaeological finding.

Whether the legends remember real outsiders is argued the same way. Jens Andreas Friis launched that reading in Lappisk Mythologi in 1871, taking the iron clothing and the raiding as memory of Norse settlers and of tax collectors. Rolf Kjellström restated it in Fataburen in 1976. Eldar Heide rejects the whole approach in 2019, because the midwinter Stállu overlaps too closely with Wild Host traditions, and those are not historical.

The name is disputed too. The standard derivation takes Stállu from Sámi stálli, steel, and it was held by Helland in 1906, Aikio in 1907, Nils Lid in 1933 and Ernst Manker in 1960. Eldar Heide rejected it in 2019 on a practical objection: medieval steel went into cutting edges, not into mail, so a steel-clad giant is the wrong picture for the period. He proposes Old Norse stál in the sense of a packed mass of living creatures, which ties Stállu to the Wild Host. That is one scholar against a century of agreement, and it is set down here as such.

Much early recording was done by missionaries actively working to suppress Sámi religion, which affects both what was written down and how. This is a case where the collection history is part of the evidence and needs stating. One claim that circulates does not survive checking. That Sámi giants and people are both descended from the Sun is not in Turi. It comes from Anders Fjellner's nineteenth century epic poems, and K. B. Wiklund challenged their fidelity to oral tradition in 1906.

fate: Consistently outwitted rather than killed; usually simply defeated.

name: Ojáncanu
shortDescription: One-eyed Cantabrian giant of the forest: enemy of the good anjana.
fullDescription: The ojáncanu is a roughly ten-foot, one-eyed giant of Cantabrian mythology: red-bearded, forest-dwelling, destructive to livestock and people, often given extra fingers as a mark of excess. His female counterpart, the ojáncana, is sometimes fiercer still.
mysteryNote: One eye, many fingers. Count the cattle twice at dusk, and thank the anjana if you still can.
sources: Manuel Llano, Cantabrian folk tales and regional writings (early 20th c.)
Regional folklore collections of Cantabria, 19th-20th c.
Comparative note: Homer, Odyssey IX (Polyphemus), for the one-eye motif

sections.story:
Cantabria is a narrow strip of green between the Bay of Biscay and the Picos de Europa: deep beech forest, high pasture, weather coming off the sea. The ojáncanu is what that country puts in the trees.

He is described as roughly ten feet, red-bearded, with a single eye in the middle of his forehead. Some tellings give him extra fingers or toes, a mark of excess rather than a functional detail. He lives in caves and the thickest woodland, and what he does is destroy: he tears up trees, rolls boulders onto paths, kills livestock, and is dangerous to people caught out alone. There is no bargain to be struck with him and no riddle to win. He is not a trickster figure.

His counterpart the ojáncana is in several accounts the worse of the two. She is given long breasts that she throws over her shoulders, and a habit of taking children: the shape a great many traditions give to a female ogre, though the specific inventory here is local.

Against them stand the anjanas: small, benevolent, fairy-like guardians of the highlands who help travellers, reward generosity and repair what the ojáncanu breaks. The pairing is the point. Cantabrian folklore sets a destroying force and a mending one in the same forest, and the forest is where people actually had to work.

A common motif holds that the ojáncanu cannot die while a single white hair remains in his beard, which gives villagers something to search for over the body.
sections.origins:
This material was collected comparatively late, and that shapes what we have.

The ojáncanu belongs to a body of Cantabrian tradition assembled mainly by nineteenth and twentieth-century folklorists working in the region's villages. Manuel Llano (1898-1938), a Cantabrian writer who drew directly on the oral culture of the Pas and Cabuérniga valleys, is the figure most responsible for carrying these beings into print, and much later popular writing traces back to him.

That gives the material a particular character. It is genuinely traditional, but it reaches us already selected and shaped by writers with a literary purpose and, in the period concerned, an interest in regional identity. The ojáncanu appears in modern Cantabrian tourism, festivals and children's books, and the line between inherited story and twentieth-century consolidation is not always drawable.
sections.disputed:
The resemblance to Polyphemus is the obvious question, and there is no agreement on what it means.

A single central eye, a cave, flocks and hostility to travellers describe both. Northern Spain was under Roman administration for centuries and classical material was certainly available, so direct literary influence is possible. It is equally possible that the pairing of one eye with mountain danger is simply a shape that recurs: the same motif turns up in Tiwi tradition in northern Australia, where Roman transmission is not on the table.

How much of the current figure is old is also unresolved. Nineteenth-century regional folklore across Europe was frequently tidied, and sometimes enlarged, by the people recording it. The ojáncanu as he now appears in print is at minimum a collaboration between village tradition and its collectors.

fate: Said to die only once every white hair is found in his beard.

name: Rübezahl
shortDescription: Mountain spirit of the Riesengebirge: trickster, giant, weather-lord.
fullDescription: Rübezahl is the weather-spirit of the Krkonoše mountains on the Czech-Polish border. He rewards the honest, punishes the arrogant, and takes violent offence at his own name.
mysteryNote: Never mock him by counting turnips. The joke is not his. It was printed in 1783, and the anger is older than the joke.
sources: Martin Helwig, map of Silesia (1561): early depiction
Johannes Praetorius, Rübezahl collections (17th c.)
J.K.A. Musäus, Volksmährchen der Deutschen, vol. 2 (1783)
Czech Krakonoš tradition, incl. Krkonošské pohádky

sections.story:
The Giant Mountains have their own governor, and he is not consistent.

Rübezahl (Krakonoš in Czech, Liczyrzepa in Polish) is the lord of the range, appearing as a giant, a monk, a miner, a hunter or an old man, and moving weather around at will. To honest travellers, poor herb-gatherers and lost children he is generous: he shows the path, fills a basket with leaves that turn to gold, cures the sick. To the proud, the greedy and the dishonest he is dangerous, and the same leaves turn back to leaves.

He is best known for one thing: he detests his German name. Calling him Rübezahl within his mountains provokes storms, landslides and pursuit. This makes the name a folkloric hazard, and much of the tradition consists of people using it and regretting it.

The name is usually explained by a story in which he abducts a princess and, to distract her, transforms turnips into copies of her friends. The turnips wither, she asks him to count them all, and escapes while he is counting. Rübezahl then reads as turnip-counter, a mocking name, and that is given as the reason he objects.

The dates do not support it. The tale is Musäus's and it is printed in 1783. Praetorius had already headed a chapter "Rübezahl kann seinen Namen nicht leiden" more than a century earlier. The Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache treats the turnip-counting story as Musäus writing tongue in cheek, not as an etymology. The anger at the name is older than the joke that explains it.

The region has kept him thoroughly. He is on tourist signage, in place-names, in Czech and Polish and German children's literature, and in a substantial body of art. A mountain spirit who punishes arrogance has proven very adaptable, and he is one of the few figures in this codex who is simultaneously a folk belief, a national mascot in three languages, and a marketing asset.
sections.origins:
The tradition is documented from the sixteenth century. Martin Helwig's map of Silesia, printed in 1561, carries a horned and hooved figure labelled Rübenczal near Sněžka. That is the first known depiction.

Johannes Praetorius, born Hans Schultze in 1630, gathered roughly 250 stories in Daemonologia Rubinzalii Silesii, three volumes, Leipzig 1662 to 1665. That is where the bulk of the material is fixed in print.

Johann Karl August Musäus published the Rübezahl legends in volume 2 of Volksmährchen der Deutschen in 1783, not 1786 as is often repeated. It is the version that shaped later German literary treatment, and it is where the turnip-counting tale comes from.

The Czech and Polish traditions did not develop in parallel with the German one. They came later. The Czech name Krakonoš is first used by Václav Kliment Klicpera in 1824. The Polish Liczyrzepa is a translation of the German name.
sections.disputed:
The origin of the name is not settled. The turnip-counting story is generally regarded as a later folk etymology attached to an already-existing name whose meaning had become opaque.

Whether Rübezahl derives from a pre-Christian mountain deity, a personification of alpine weather, or a comparatively late literary construction is argued. The sixteenth-century first attestation is a real constraint on claims of great antiquity, though absence of earlier record is not proof of absence.

The three national traditions have diverged and each has been shaped by its own cultural politics, particularly in the twentieth century when the region's population changed radically. The German Rübezahl, Czech Krakonoš and Polish Liczyrzepa are no longer quite the same figure.

All three national names are late. Rübenczal is on the map in 1561 and the German material is collected from 1662. Krakonoš is Klicpera's, from 1824. Liczyrzepa translates the German. Mateusz J. Hartwich has documented how the teacher Józef Sykulski, who settled in Hirschberg in 1945, set out to make the mountain spirit a Pole. The figure three countries argue over was assembled in print between 1662 and 1824.

fate: No death: still rules the Giant Mountains under different names.

name: Giant of Kandahar
shortDescription: Unverified modern military legend of a red-haired giant near Kandahar.
fullDescription: The Giant of Kandahar is a story that a US special forces team killed a red-haired, six-fingered giant in Afghanistan in 2002. There is no evidence for it, and the story's actual history is documentable.
mysteryNote: War makes large shadows. Not every shadow has a body that a laboratory has held, or that paperwork admits.
sources: Paranormal radio and internet forum circulation, mid-2000s onward
Cable television treatments, 2010s (amplification, not evidence)
Absence of corroborating US military records; reported FOIA results
Comparative: 19th-c. American giant lore and Nephilim literature

sections.story:
The claim, as it circulates, is specific enough to sound like a report. A US special operations patrol goes missing in Kandahar province. A second team is sent, finds a cave, and encounters a giant: variously twelve to fifteen feet tall, red-haired, with six fingers on each hand and two rows of teeth. It kills one soldier with a spear before being shot. The body is flown out and everything is classified.

None of this is supported by anything.

What can be traced is where the story came from. It surfaced through paranormal talk radio and internet forums in the 2000s, gained wide circulation through repetition, and was substantially amplified by cable television treatments in the 2010s. The named witnesses are anonymous or unverifiable. No unit, no date, no casualty record, and no serviceman has ever been identified. US military casualties in Afghanistan are documented in detail, and no death matches the account.

The physical details are worth noticing because they are not random. Red hair, six fingers and double rows of teeth are the standard inventory of nineteenth-century American giant lore and of the Nephilim literature: the same features attached to the Lovelock Cave claims elsewhere in this codex. The Kandahar story is assembled from an existing kit.

Its persistence is the genuinely interesting part: a war zone that is closed to verification, a claim of classification that makes absence of evidence into evidence, and an audience for whom the giants of Genesis are a live proposition.

We include it because the codex covers modern legend, and this is a clean specimen of one forming in traceable conditions. It is not a report of an event.
sections.origins:
The story has no primary source. Its documented history runs through paranormal radio programming and internet forums from the mid-2000s onward.

Cable television treatments, particularly in the 2010s, gave it mass circulation and are the route by which most people encountered it.

No military record, casualty report, unit history or named participant supports it. Freedom of Information requests reported by journalists have produced nothing.

Its component details derive from a long tradition of American giant lore and from Nephilim literature, both of which are documented and considerably older.
sections.disputed:
There is nothing to dispute in the ordinary sense. No evidence has been produced in more than two decades.

The classification claim is unfalsifiable by design, and that is a recognised feature of this kind of story rather than an argument in its favour.

What is genuinely worth studying is the transmission: how a claim with no source acquires circumstantial detail, named-sounding witnesses and television airtime. The Kandahar story is unusually well documented as a case of that process because it happened recently and online.

Treating this entry as evidence of anything other than how modern legends form would be a misreading of it.

fate: No verified fate: the claim has no primary source at all.

name: Giant of Kunar
shortDescription: Unverified legend of a giant observed in Kunar Province.
fullDescription: A parallel Afghanistan story places a giant in the Kunar valley. Like the Kandahar version, it has no verifiable source, and the two accounts have merged in circulation.
mysteryNote: Two provinces. One pattern of rumor. Zero paperwork, and a codex that refuses to launder rumor as fact.
sources: Paranormal radio and internet forum circulation, mid-2000s onward
Cable television treatments, 2010s (amplification, not evidence)
Absence of corroborating military records

sections.story:
The Kunar story runs on the same lines as the Kandahar one: a remote valley, a cave, a patrol, an enormous being, casualties, a recovered body, classification.

In practice the two are frequently told as one. Details migrate between them (the red hair, the six fingers, the spear), and different retellings place the same events in different provinces. That instability is itself informative. A report has a location; a legend has a setting, and settings are interchangeable.

Kunar province is mountainous, remote, and was among the harder areas of the Afghan conflict. It is exactly the kind of place a story like this attaches to: difficult terrain, limited access, genuine danger, and a long history of outside forces failing to control it.

Everything said about the Kandahar version applies here. There is no unit, no date, no casualty, no witness who can be identified, and no document. The claim that the evidence is classified performs the same function of insulating the story from checking.

What makes the pair worth keeping in a codex like this one is that they show a legend in its formative phase. Most of the entries here reach us through centuries of transmission with the origins lost. These two are perhaps twenty years old, they formed in public on recorded media, and the process can be watched.

They are also a reminder of the disclaimer this site carries on every modern-legend entry: unverified oral tradition is not a weaker kind of fact. It is a different kind of thing.
sections.origins:
No primary source exists, and that is the finding rather than a gap in our research.

Circulation runs through the same paranormal radio and internet ecosystem as the Kandahar story, from the mid-2000s onward. The earliest traceable appearances are forum posts and call-in segments, neither of which cite anything, and each subsequent retelling cites the previous one.

Television treatments in the 2010s carried both versions, frequently without distinguishing them, and are responsible for most of the story's present reach. Broadcast is not corroboration, though it is regularly mistaken for it.

No military documentation, casualty record, unit history or identifiable witness exists for either version. US deaths in Afghanistan are individually documented and none matches.

The two stories have substantially merged in retelling, and many accounts cannot now be assigned to one or the other.
sections.disputed:
Whether Kunar and Kandahar were ever distinct stories is unclear. They may have separate origins that converged, or one may be a relocated version of the other.

As with Kandahar, there is no evidence to weigh. The appropriate description is not "unproven" but "unsourced".

The value of the entry is documentary: it records that these claims exist and how they spread, not that anything happened.

Readers encountering confident retellings with specific details should note that specificity in this material tends to increase with distance from any source, which is the reverse of how evidence behaves.

fate: No verified fate: the claim has no primary source at all.

name: Paul Bunyan
height: As tall as the tale requires
shortDescription: Lumberjack giant of American tall tales: Babe the Blue Ox at his side.
fullDescription: Paul Bunyan is a giant lumberjack with a blue ox named Babe. He is the best-known giant in American folklore and substantially an advertising creation, which is the most interesting thing about him.
mysteryNote: The ox is blue because the winter was cold. Or because the story required it. On the frontier, that was evidence enough.
sources: Great Lakes logging-camp oral tradition, late 19th c.
James MacGillivray, Detroit News-Tribune (1910)
William Laughead, Red River Lumber Company pamphlets (1916 onward)
Richard Dorson, on fakelore (mid-20th c. critique)
imageAlt: Paul Bunyan and Babe the Blue Ox

sections.story:
The Paul Bunyan of popular knowledge scoops out the Great Lakes to water Babe, drags his axe behind him and gouges the Grand Canyon, and creates the ten thousand lakes of Minnesota with his and Babe's footprints. He clears forests at impossible speed. His griddle is greased by men skating across it with bacon strapped to their feet.

None of it asks to be believed. The tall tale is a genre with its own contract: the teller exaggerates, the listener knows, and the pleasure is in the escalation. This makes Bunyan structurally different from every other entry in this codex. He is not a belief that faded into story. He was a joke from the beginning.

His origins are genuinely in the logging camps of the Great Lakes region and eastern Canada, where oral tall tales about an outsized lumberjack circulated among workers in the later nineteenth century. That much is accepted.

What happened next is unusual. In 1916 the Red River Lumber Company, a California logging firm, began publishing promotional pamphlets written by an advertising man named William Laughead, featuring Paul Bunyan as a mascot. Laughead invented a great deal: Babe the Blue Ox appears to be substantially his, along with several of the supporting characters and much of the material now considered traditional.

The advertising Bunyan then escaped into general culture and became folklore in reverse: a commercial character absorbed into the national repertoire, taught in schools, and commemorated in enormous roadside statues across the northern United States.

Folklorists have argued about him for a century, with some calling the whole thing fakelore. He is a giant made of marketing that people genuinely adopted.
sections.origins:
Oral tall tales among lumber workers in the Great Lakes region and eastern Canada, later nineteenth century, are the genuine substrate. Documentation of this phase is thin.

Early print appearances include a 1910 newspaper piece by James MacGillivray in the Detroit News-Tribune.

William Laughead's promotional pamphlets for the Red River Lumber Company, from 1916 onward, are the decisive intervention and introduced much of the now-standard material including Babe.

Later literary treatments by Esther Shephard, James Stevens and others consolidated the figure. Richard Dorson's critique, coining the term fakelore, is the central scholarly intervention.
sections.disputed:
How much of Bunyan is authentically traditional and how much is Laughead's is the long-running argument. The oral substrate is accepted; its content is poorly documented, which makes the boundary hard to draw.

Richard Dorson's charge of fakelore has been influential and also contested. Critics argue that the distinction between authentic and commercial tradition is less clean than Dorson allowed, and that material genuinely adopted by a public is folklore whatever its origin.

Regional claims to Bunyan's origin (Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Maine, Quebec) are numerous, competitive and mostly commercially motivated.

Some early logging-camp material was rough and, by modern standards, offensive in ways later versions removed. The sanitised children's Bunyan is itself a further layer of construction.

fate: No death: a tall tale does not require one.

name: Surtr
shortDescription: The fire giant who guarded the world's edge before it existed, and will burn it down at the end.
fullDescription: Where Ymir has an origin, Surtr has none. He is already there: a fire giant standing guard at the border of Muspellheim since before the ordered cosmos began, waiting for the day he leads the sons of Muspell against the gods and burns the nine worlds to ash.
mysteryNote: The lava tube in Iceland that bears his name is still there, and still warm in places no one can explain. Locals stopped naming which places those are.
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning (Iceland, c. 1220)
Poetic Edda: Völuspá, stanzas 51-53
Surtshellir archaeological surveys (Iceland)
imageAlt: Surtr, the fire giant of Muspellheim

sections.story:
Unlike Ymir, Surtr has no origin story. He is simply already there, guarding the border of Muspellheim since before the ordered cosmos began. Where Ymir's whole existence is explained in careful, sequential detail, Surtr is only ever described in terms of his function: a fixed point of destruction at the edge of the world.

At Ragnarök, he leads the sons of Muspell against the gods, kills Freyr, and sets the entire world ablaze with his flaming sword, said to shine brighter than the sun itself. He is Ymir's structural mirror: a primordial being from the opposite element, present at both the beginning and the end of the world, but where Ymir dies so the world can be built, Surtr survives to burn that same world down.

The Prose Edda's Gylfaginning describes Surtr conversationally, alongside Muspell, rather than placing him in a creation sequence. Even the text's own structure resists giving him a timeline. He is just already there, waiting.
sections.origins: Surtr's textual footprint is thin compared to Ymir's, and it is scattered across sources of different kinds and dates. The Poetic Edda's Völuspá, the oldest and most authoritative account of Ragnarök, places him at the final battle: he comes from the south bearing fire, and the sun goes black once his flame has done its work. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, compiled in Iceland around 1220, gives the fuller narrative context in Gylfaginning, where Surtr is introduced as already guarding Muspellheim's border, alongside a description of Muspell itself as a realm of fire predating the ordered world. Snorri is working roughly two centuries after Iceland's conversion, synthesising oral and poetic material that had already fragmented by the time it reached him.
sections.disputed: It is sometimes asked whether Gylfaginning's placement of Surtr alongside Muspell during the account of creation implies he predates Ymir. The stronger reading is that it does not: Gylfaginning is framed as a dialogue between Hár, Jafnhár and Þriði on one side and Gylfi on the other, so topics surface as they become conversationally relevant rather than in strict chronological order. Describing Surtr as already present at that point in the exchange states what exists at the time of narration, not a creation sequence. A separate, older uncertainty concerns Muspell itself: the Eddas are not fully consistent about whether it names a place, a being, or a people, and that ambiguity extends to how precisely Surtr's own role within it should be understood.

fate: Leads the sons of Muspell at Ragnarök and burns the nine worlds to ash.

scholarlyNotes.heading: A being with no origin
scholarlyNotes.body: Surtr is Ymir's structural mirror in Norse cosmology: a primordial being present at both the beginning and the end of the world. But where Ymir's origin is described in careful, sequential detail (his formation from meltwater, his death, the construction of the world from his body), Surtr has no origin story at all. He is simply already present, guarding the border of Muspellheim, and will still be standing there to burn the world down at Ragnarök. Ymir dies so the ordered world can be built; Surtr survives to end that same world.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Why the sources don't place him on a timeline
scholarlyNotes.body: It is sometimes asked whether the Prose Edda's Gylfaginning implies Surtr existed before Ymir, since he is mentioned alongside Muspell during the account of creation. The stronger reading is that this is not the case. Gylfaginning is structured as a conversation between Hár, Jafnhár, and Þriði on one side and Gylfi on the other, so topics are introduced as they become conversationally relevant, not necessarily in chronological order. Mentioning that Surtr already guards Muspellheim's border at that point in the dialogue describes what exists at the time of narration; it does not assert a creation sequence. This fits the broader pattern above: Surtr is treated as a fixed, ever-present guardian rather than a being with a beginning, and even the structure of the source text resists placing him on a timeline.

scholarlyNotes.heading: A physical trace: Surtshellir
scholarlyNotes.body: Unlike most figures in the Norse corpus, Surtr has a documented physical site associated with his name: Surtshellir, a lava tube in Iceland literally named after him. The site shows archaeological evidence of activity dating to the pagan period, with later fortification. This is unusually direct: most Norse deities exist almost entirely in text, but Surtshellir suggests active cultic association with a specific, visitable location, not simply a name applied after the fact.

name: Ispolini
shortDescription: Bulgaria's giants were God's second attempt at people. We are the third.
fullDescription: God made three attempts at people, and the dwarves were too small to survive. The ispolini were the correction.
mysteryNote: The word may be the name of a nation the Goths destroyed.
sources: Стойнев, Попов, Василева and Попов, "Исполини", Българска митология: Енциклопедичен речник, 2006
Атанас Илиев, Български предания за исполини, наречени елини, жидови и латини, Сборник за народни умотворения 3, 1890
Макс Фасмер, "исполин", Этимологический словарь русского языка, 1964 to 1973, for the Spali derivation and for Meillet's objection
Jordanes and Pliny the Elder as cited there
imageAlt: Ispolini, the Bulgarian giants of the second creation

sections.story:
Bulgarian tradition places its giants inside a full sequence. The first people God made were dwarves, and they were too small to defend themselves from wild animals or to work the land, so they died out. To replace them God made the ispolini, deliberately as the opposite. We are the third attempt.

They stood up to three metres with enormous heads, though the regional variants differ: some give them three heads, some a single eye the size of an egg set in the forehead, some a single leg. They lived in the mountains and in caves before history and ate their meat raw. They fought dragons. Their voices carried so far that two of them could hold a conversation from separate mountaintops.

And they were frightened of blackberries. The danger was tripping over the brambles and dying, and so the ispolini made sacrifices to the plant.
sections.origins:
The word is old, and where it comes from is an argument rather than a fact. Ispolin appears meaning giant in Old Church Slavonic texts of Rus by the eleventh century. Max Vasmer derived it from the Spali, a people the Goths defeated somewhere north of the Black Sea. Jordanes records that defeat in the sixth century, and Pliny the Elder had already listed a people called Spalaei in the same region in the first.

If Vasmer is right, the Bulgarian word for a giant is the name of a nation that lost, which is the same move the folklore itself makes when it calls its giants Greeks and Latins.

He was not unopposed. Antoine Meillet argued that the initial vowel points to the word reaching Slavic through a Romance intermediary rather than directly from the ethnonym. Vasmer went through the other proposals and turned down each: a Greek Asphaloi, a Celtic Spali, a Turkic Spali, a link to Old Icelandic spjalla, and the folk reading that hears the Slavic word for field inside it.

There is a peak in the Balkan range called Ispolin.
sections.disputed: The names given to them are worth pausing on. Atanas Iliev's 1890 collection is titled, in translation, Bulgarian legends about the ispolini, called Greeks, Jews and Latins. Romanian tradition does the same thing, calling its giants jidovi, novaci and tătari. Two neighbouring traditions independently naming their prehistoric giants after historical neighbouring peoples. The giant here is not only the one who came before. He is the one who is not us, and the vocabulary gets borrowed from whoever the nearest outsider happens to be.

fate: Replaced. They were the second of three attempts, and we are the third.

name: Gargantua
shortDescription: Folk giant older than Rabelais: over four hundred French megaliths and rocks are named for him.
fullDescription: Rabelais did not invent him. The name was already in use as a nickname in 1470, and by then the countryside was full of his furniture.
mysteryNote: He left his quoit, his chair and his bowl lying about across France, and never came back for them. The Church renamed them for the devil, and the stones stayed exactly where they were.
sources: Paul Sébillot, Gargantua dans les traditions populaires, Maisonneuve, Paris, 1883
Félix Bourquelot, 1844
Henri Gaidoz
Henri Dontenville
Guy-Édouard Pillard, Le Vrai Gargantua: mythologie d'un géant, 1987
Les grandes et inestimables chroniques du grand et énorme géant Gargantua, anonymous, 1532

sections.story:
Across rural France, standing stones and strange rock formations carry his name and, more precisely, the names of his belongings. His quoit. His distaff. His skittle. His chair, his armchair, his bowl, his gravel. Sébillot, Dontenville and their successors catalogued more than four hundred such place-names, under regional variants including Grand-Tua, Grand-Tuard, Guergintua, Jergantua, Gargountoun and Gargantoua.

This is the megalith tradition at its largest recorded scale anywhere. Not a vanished race who raised the stones, but one named giant who left his things lying about.

The case that he predates literature was made by the palaeographer Félix Bourquelot in 1844 and settled by the Breton ethnologist Paul Sébillot, who in the 1880s sent a questionnaire to mythographers and local scholars across the country and published the returns in 1883. George Sand had already said it plainly: Gargantua is the work of the people, and Rabelais, like every great creator, took his material where he found it.

Then the Church took the landscape back. The places, the chasms, the rock chaoses and the standing stones called Gargantua's were rebaptised as the devil's, and the giant was set against Christian figures. The stones did not move. Only the owner's name changed.

He grew so large in the popular imagination that he absorbed the local giants around him, and anonymous or half-remembered figures across France ended up with his name attached. A few escaped: Roland in the Basque country, Hok Bras and Rannou in Lower Brittany.
sections.origins:
The literary Gargantua reaches print in 1532, in the anonymous chapbook *Les grandes et inestimables chroniques du grand et énorme géant Gargantua*, printed at Lyon, alongside Rabelais's own books of the 1530s. The folk figure is older, and it was recovered by nineteenth-century collectors rather than by literary scholarship.

Félix Bourquelot set out the case for a Gargantua preceding Rabelais in a notice of 1844, published in the Mémoires de la Société des antiquaires de France. Henri Gaidoz followed in 1868 with *Gargantua, essai de mythologie celtique*, a paper read to the Société de linguistique de Paris in the sessions of 6 and 20 June that year.

Paul Sébillot's *Gargantua dans les traditions populaires* (Maisonneuve, Paris, 1883) gathered the returns of his circulated questionnaire into the standard collection. Henri Dontenville, founder in 1950 of the Société de mythologie française, and Guy-Édouard Pillard, in *Le Vrai Gargantua* (Imago, 1987), carried the survey forward.
sections.disputed: Sébillot read the name as meaning the devourer. Later scholarship prefers something closer to the fierce or the wild. Some argue Gargantua is the residue of a Celtic god named Gargan, but there is no archaeological trace supporting that, and at least one popular etymology used to support it, reading the islet name Tombelaine as containing a Gaulish god's name, does not hold: the name derives from an older form built on *Tumba*.

fate: No death: he absorbed the local giants around him, and his stones were rebaptised as the devil's.

name: Mouros
shortDescription: Builders of the megaliths of north-west Iberia: unbaptised people of the earth whose name may mean the dead.
fullDescription: They raised the standing stones in a single night, and their name may mean the dead.
mysteryNote: The stones were standing before morning. Whoever set them there went under the ground, and did not come back up.
sources: Isidoro Millán on the etymology
Galician and Asturian folk collections
the mouros are also documented under Portuguese tradition as the moura encantada

sections.story:
The mouros are found across Galicia, Asturias, León, Zamora and northern Portugal. They are described as unbaptised and pagan, and in older usage they were also called xentís, the same word the Basques use for their own megalith builders.

Every mámoa, every burial tumulus, every castro, every Roman mine, and by extension every ruin of unremembered origin is theirs. Some accounts have them raising the stones overnight. They live underground now and rarely come out, except to fetch food and at midsummer. Their money is enchanted and disappears after it is spent.

The mouras, the women, are pale from living beneath the earth or the water, blue-eyed, and guard treasure. They can take other shapes and most often choose the serpent. Some of them could fly, and carried the stones through the air themselves. Bargains made with them and then broken bring blindness, barrenness, or ruin on a family line.

The philologist Isidoro Millán derived the word not from *moro*, Moor, but from a Celtic form *mrvos*, related to the Indo-European *mr-tuos* that gives Latin *mortuus*. On that reading the people who built the old stones and live under the ground are named, quite literally, the dead. The confusion with the Moors came later, after the Muslim conquest, and runs the wrong way round.
sections.origins:
No medieval text stands behind the mouros. The tradition is oral, and reaches print only through nineteenth and twentieth century collectors.

In Portugal José Leite de Vasconcelos gathered the material from Tradições populares de Portugal (1882) onward and returned to it in Opúsculos, volume V, Etnologia (Lisbon: Imprensa Nacional, 1938). Zófimo Consiglieri Pedroso read the mouras as water spirits. Revista Lusitana, the journal Leite de Vasconcelos founded, printed Abílio Brandão's "Lendas de Mouras encantadas" in volume XIV (1911). The archaeologist Francisco Martins Sarmento treated the legends as a guide to unexcavated monuments.

Asturian versions were collected by Aurelio de Llano Roza de Ampudia in Del folklore asturiano: mitos, supersticiones, costumbres (1922). Galician versions run through the ethnographic writing of Vicente Risco and later collections such as Camiño Noia's Contos galegos de tradición oral. Alexandre Parafita's A Mitologia dos Mouros (Porto: Gailivro, 2006) is the modern Portuguese synthesis.

The Celtic etymology is a philological proposal by Isidoro Millán González-Pardo (1922 to 2002), not a folk claim.
sections.disputed: Whether the mouros are properly giants at all. Some accounts describe them as enormous, others as living much as ordinary Galician peasants did. The mouros encantados sometimes appear as giants or warriors, and a separate tradition of mourinhos describes very small underground people instead. They are best understood as the previous inhabitants rather than as a size.

fate: Went underground with the stones they raised, and stayed there.

name: Dragonja
shortDescription: Istrian giant who ploughed the Mirna into being; his kind built the hill towns.
fullDescription: He dragged a plough from the mountains to the sea. Water followed the furrow, and he named it Mirna.
mysteryNote: You can walk the whole of his day's work between breakfast and dusk, and the furrow still has water in it. Only the giants are missing.
sources: Maja Bošković-Stulli, Istarske narodne priče
Carlo De Franceschi, who recorded giant traditions around Motovun

sections.story:
Before people settled Istria, the valley of the Mirna belonged to giants. The chief among them was Dragonja, called the Ploughman, because he cut the furrow from Ćićarija down to the coast and let the river in. The border river Dragonja still carries his name.

The giants built the hill towns: Motovun, Vrh, Sovinjak, Oprtalj, Završje, Roč and Grožnjan. They were so large that each worked his own hilltop and they passed tools and building stone to one another across the valleys between. When the towns were finished there was stone left over, and rather than waste it they built one more. That is Hum, which now advertises itself as the smallest town in the world.

After the work they rested at Kotli, where the water falls in steps and where people still walk today.

Dragonja's son Gorazd is said to be in the forests of the Istrian highlands still, watching them.

Set him beside Daidarabotchi in Japan. Both are giants who made a real, named, walkable landscape by working on it while they were alive, which is the opposite of Ymir, who had to die first.
sections.origins:
This is local place-legend from the Mirna valley in central Istria, tied to named ground rather than to any medieval text: the rivers Mirna and Dragonja, the hill towns above them, the water steps at Kotli.

Nineteenth-century collecting in Istria concentrated on song. The circle around the newspaper Naša sloga gathered oral material from 1879, printed as Hrvatske narodne pjesme što se pjevaju po Istri i Kvarnerskih otocih in 1880, and Jakov Volčić recorded songs, tales and proverbs. Prose legend was the poorer relation. Carlo De Franceschi (1809 to 1893), historian of Istria and secretary of the Istrian Diet from 1861 to 1876, is the name cited for giant traditions from the Motovun district.

Systematic prose collecting came in the 1950s, when the Institut za narodnu umjetnost in Zagreb, now the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research, worked across the peninsula. Maja Bošković-Stulli edited the result as Istarske narodne priče (Zagreb, 1959), the first volume of the series Narodno stvaralaštvo Istre, with her introduction and commentary.

The tradition now travels largely through local tourism, which has an interest in it.
sections.disputed: The most famous Istrian giant, Veli Jože, is not folk tradition. He comes from Vladimir Nazor's novel of 1908, which draws on Istrian material but is an authored work written with a national awakening in mind. He is frequently presented as ancient. He is not.

fate: No death recorded. His son Gorazd is said to watch the Istrian highlands still.

name: Daidarabotchi
shortDescription: Japanese landscape giant: Fuji is his spoil heap, Lake Biwa the hole it came from.
fullDescription: Mount Fuji is the soil he dug out of one province. Lake Biwa is the hole he left in another.
mysteryNote: No one records a single word he said. Everything known about him is the shape he left in the ground: a lake, a mountain, and a plateau where he lay down.
sources: Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, 8th century
Kunio Yanagita, "The Footprints of Daidarabou", Chūō Kōron, 1927, the first systematic collection of the scattered footprint legends

sections.story:
Daidarabotchi is a giant of the Kantō and Chūbu regions, known also as Deidarabotchi, Derabotchi and Daidarabō depending on where the story is told. That spread of names is itself evidence: separate local traditions arriving at the same figure.

He built Fuji from earth he scooped out of Kai Province, which is why the land around the mountain is a wide basin. When he needed more he dug again in Ōmi, and that pit filled with water and became Lake Biwa, the largest lake in Japan. He once picked up Fuji and Tsukuba to weigh them against each other and split Tsukuba's summit doing it.

Senba Lake in Ibaraki fills a single one of his footprints. The Takabocchi Plateau in Nagano is where he lay down to rest his back. The towns of Daita and Daitakubo carry his name. The earliest textual trace is in the eighth-century *Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki*, which records a giant seated on a hill eating clams from the beach and piling the shells into mounds.

Unlike almost everything else in this catalogue, he is not a threat. In Ibaraki he is remembered warmly, as a giant who shifted mountains to make life easier for the people below. He is felt through the ground he left behind rather than through any encounter.
sections.origins:
The oldest written trace is the Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, one of the provincial gazetteers ordered by the edict of 713 and compiled in the decade after it. Its Naka district notice describes a giant on the hill at Ōkushi who reached from the hilltop to the shore for clams, the discarded shells becoming the hill itself. That hill is the Ōgushi shell mound at Shiozaki in Mito, a real Jōmon midden, protected as a national historic site since 1970. The giant there is called only ōhito, a great person. The Harima no Kuni Fudoki carries a comparable figure whose footprints filled with water and became marshes.

The name Daidarabotchi belongs to later oral tradition. Ryūtei Tanehiko noted the word in his miscellany Yōshabako, printed in 1841. The scattered local legends were first gathered as a single body of material by Yanagita Kunio in "Daidarabō no ashiato", published in Chūō Kōron in April 1927 and collected in Hitotsume Kozō sono ta (Koyama Shoten, 1934).
sections.disputed:
The etymology is unsettled. Ryūtei Tanehiko, in his miscellany Yōshabako of 1841, took the word as an insult aimed at large men, the inverse of Issun-bōshi, the one-inch boy. Yanagita derived it from Daitarō-hōshi and read the tara element as an old term of respect for a person of rank. Minakata Kumagusu took daida as a contraction of the personal name Daitarō. A separate proposal, recorded in the Nipponica encyclopedia beside Yanagita's own, links tara to tatara, the foot-bellows of iron smelting, and reads the giant as a trace of the spread of smiths.

What he originally was is also argued. Watanabe Shōgo's Nipponica article on giant legends treats him as a land-making god degraded into a comic figure as belief fell away, in company with oni and tengu. The reverse account, a yōkai tradition swelling into a giant one, also has currency.

The fudoki giants are not named Daidarabotchi. They are ōhito, great people, and the Hitachi text survives only in an abridged recension.

fate: No death: he is felt through the ground he left behind rather than through any encounter.

name: Baqbaq-Devi
shortDescription: Many-headed giants of the Georgian mountains: their strongest was outriddled, not outfought.
fullDescription: Cut off a devi's head and another grows. So the hero did not bring a sword. He brought a riddle.
mysteryNote: Cut one head and another answers. So the hero came carrying a question instead, and kept asking until the last head slept.
sources: Kartlis Tskhovreba
Dodona Kiziria, "Amirani: A Georgian Folk Hero", Folklore Forum 7, no. 7, 1974, p. 133
living oral tradition of the Georgian highlands, Christianised roughly ten centuries later than the lowlands

sections.story:
The devi are the giants of the Georgian mountains. They are many-headed, and a severed head simply grows back, which is why Georgian heroes do not win these fights by force. They win by outthinking them, or by striking at the heart.

They live underground or high in the remote Caucasus peaks, usually as a family of seven or nine brothers in a castle with their wives, their children and their hoard. When the ground shakes and a hillside tears loose, that is them.

The strongest of all of them was Baqbaq-Devi, the one the other giants deferred to. Amirani, the great Georgian culture hero, could not beat him in a straight fight and did not try. He challenged the giant to a contest of riddles instead, and used the rhythm of his own voice to put the many heads to sleep one after another. Then he stabbed him through the heart.
